passage:
Dear Farhan,
City school, month two. The building has lifts! But I want to tell you the other thing.
On day one, a boy asked if we had electricity "back there". Last week Ma'am read my essay aloud and said, "Very good, especially for someone from a village school." Everyone clapped. Today in the lab a girl said, "You speak English so well, where did you learn?" I said, "In school, like you." She looked surprised.
None of them is cruel. I know that. But I keep counting them, like pebbles in my shoe. By evening my feet hurt from pebbles I can't show anyone.
Did anyone say things like this to you when you moved for college?
Tell your mother the essay was about her mango tree. Write soon.
Ganga

qa.a: "Very good, especially for someone from a village school."

qa.a: Ganga feels each remark is tiny, but they keep piling up and hurting in a way that's hard to show anyone.

qa.a: Ganga could keep writing to Farhan, or tell a trusted teacher how the "especially for" comments feel, so the weight is shared.

qa.q: How might the girl in the lab have felt when Ganga said "In school, like you"?
qa.a: She may have been surprised, and perhaps briefly noticed that her question assumed something about Ganga.

grounding: A teenager new to a city school describes small, repeated remarks about a village background and English, adding up to feeling like an outsider.

passage: You want to know why I stopped answering in class, Sarita? It's not one big thing. It's small ones. passage: On the crowded evening metro, Arnab noticed the man in the grey jacket again. He had been standing too close to Gopika, Arnab's classmate, for two stations, leaning in whenever the train swayed and muttering something. Gopika kept shifting her bag in front of her, jaw tight. Arnab's first urge was to shout at him. Instead he moved beside her and asked quietly, "Hey, is this guy bothering you? Do you want me to stand here, get off with you, or tell the guard? Your call." Gopika breathed out. "Just stand here. And get off with me at the next stop." On the platform she said, "I want to report it, but I want to do it myself." Arnab waited while she spoke to the station security officer, and only added what he had seen when she asked him to.

qa.q: What options did Arnab offer Gopika?
qa.a: To stand there, get off with her, or tell the guard: "Your call."

qa.q: What was Arnab's first urge, and why might he have held it back?
qa.a: His first urge was to shout at the man; he held back so Gopika could decide what she wanted instead of having a scene made around her.

qa.q: Why did Arnab only add what he had seen when Gopika asked?
qa.a: It kept the report in Gopika's hands, so the help supported her choice instead of taking over.

qa.q: How might Gopika have felt being asked "Your call"?
qa.a: She probably felt respected and less helpless, able to choose what would make her feel safe.

grounding: A young man who sees a classmate harassed on the metro asks her privately what she wants and follows her lead in reporting it.

passage:
"Anju, can I come in?" Elizabeth knocked on the half-open door.
Anjali was on her bed, phone face down. "You saw it."
"I saw it. What Vikas posted under your photo was disgusting. I wanted to reply to him in the group right away."
"Please don't."
"I didn't. That's why I'm here. I don't want to decide this for you. What do you want? We can report it to the warden, or to the college committee. I can come with you. Or I can just sit here and we eat biscuits and hate him."
Anjali laughed a little, then her eyes filled. "I want it gone. But I don't want a big fight in the group."
"Okay. We take screenshots, then you report it through the committee form. I'll sit with you while you fill it in."
"Tonight?"
"Whenever you say."
Anjali turned her phone over. "Tonight."

qa.q: Where did Vikas post his comment?
qa.a: Under Anjali's photo, in the group.

qa.q: Why did Anjali say "Please don't" so quickly?
qa.a: She was afraid of a big public fight in the group, which would put even more attention on her.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth choose to do instead of replying in the group, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Elizabeth came to ask what Anjali wanted and offered options, so Anjali stayed in control of how it was handled.

qa.q: How might Vikas be affected by a committee report rather than a public reply?
qa.a: A report means Vikas faces a proper process, not a public shouting match he could enjoy or twist around.

grounding: A friend who saw someone harassed online checks privately what she wants, offers reporting or company, and lets her choose.

passage: At the college fest last spring, I watched three guys from another department follow Kavitha from the food stalls to the stage, calling out comments about her dress. I was furious. My plan was to march up and tell them off in front of everyone. But I remembered the time someone "defended" me by yelling at a boy in the canteen, and how everyone then stared at me, not him. So I waited until Kavitha stepped behind the stage and asked, "Those guys are being gross. What would help? Leave, report them, or I just stick next to you?" Kavitha thought for a second. "Stick next to me. If they come back, we'll tell the fest volunteers." They came back once. We told the volunteers together. I'm Shalini, by the way. Kavitha still calls me her bodyguard, which isn't quite right. I was more like the extra seat.

qa.q: What were the three guys calling out about?
qa.a: Comments about Kavitha's dress.

qa.q: Why did Shalini decide not to march up and tell them off?
qa.a: Shalini remembered being "defended" loudly in the canteen and how everyone stared at the target, and didn't want that for Kavitha.

qa.q: What made Shalini's question behind the stage a good turning point?
qa.a: It offered clear choices, leave, report or company, and let Kavitha pick, so the help followed her lead.

qa.q: What does Kavitha calling Shalini a "bodyguard" suggest about how she experienced the help?
qa.a: She felt protected and not alone, even though what Shalini really did was stay beside her and follow her plan.

grounding: A young adult who witnesses a friend being harassed asks her privately what would help and follows her choice rather than taking over.

passage: At the tehsil office in the kasba, the clerk flicked through Minakshi's land papers and smirked. "Where's your father? Girls don't understand these matters." Before Minakshi could open her mouth, Bhavna slammed her palm on the counter. "How dare you! Do you know who she is? She's doing a B.Com!" Heads turned all down the queue. Bhavna kept going, louder, about her own cousin's case, about "people like you". The clerk's face shut like a door. Minakshi stood holding her file, feeling smaller with every word. Bhavna meant well; she knew that. She was even grateful. But she had had her answer ready, calm and exact, and now nobody would hear it. On the walk home she said, "Next time, can you stand next to me and let me talk first?" Bhavna blinked, then nodded.

qa.q: What did the clerk ask Minakshi?
qa.a: "Where's your father?", adding that girls don't understand these matters.

qa.q: Why did Minakshi feel smaller with every word Bhavna said?
qa.a: She had a calm, exact answer ready, and Bhavna's shouting took over, so her own voice was lost even though she was grateful.

qa.q: What did Minakshi's request on the walk home ask for, and why is it fair?
qa.a: She asked Bhavna to stand beside her and let her speak first, which keeps the support while leaving Minakshi in charge.

qa.q: How might Bhavna have seen the scene at the counter?
qa.a: Bhavna probably felt she was loyally standing up for her friend, and may be surprised to learn it made Minakshi feel sidelined.

grounding: A young woman targeted by a clerk's remark is defended loudly by a friend who speaks for her, and feels grateful yet smaller.

passage: At the bakery near the university in Berlin, a customer squinted at Amara's name badge and said loudly, "Where are you from? Your German's surprisingly good for..." He trailed off. Amara was about to say, drily, "For a Berliner?" when Zeynep swept in from the ovens. "Excuse me! That is racist! You can't say that to her!" The whole queue turned. Zeynep kept talking: how she'd heard this all her life, how exhausting it was, how people like him never learn. The man left. Later Zeynep hugged Amara and showed her a long post she'd written about "what happened to my coworker today". Amara thanked her, and meant it. But in the post she was just "my coworker", and the story was Zeynep's. That night she texted: "Thank you for having my back. Next time, ask me first?"

qa.q: What was Amara about to say to the customer?
qa.a: "For a Berliner?"

qa.q: Why did Amara feel uneasy about Zeynep's post even though she was thankful?
qa.a: In the post she was only "my coworker", and the story had become Zeynep's, leaving Amara grateful but sidelined.

qa.q: Was Amara's text a good way to handle it, and why?
qa.a: Yes; it thanked Zeynep honestly while asking for one clear change, being asked first, so support can follow Amara's lead next time.

qa.q: Why might Zeynep have reacted so strongly at the counter?
qa.a: Zeynep said she'd heard remarks like that all her life, so the moment may have stirred her own hurt as much as concern for Amara.

passage: At the university sports complex, Elizabeth had just walked into the nets for mixed practice when a batter called, "Wrong place, the netball court's next door." A few people snorted. Anjali, bowling at the far end, marched over. "Say that again! She's the best leg-spinner here!" Then she turned to the coach, arms waving. "This is why girls quit! Elizabeth is too polite to say anything, so I'll say it for her." Elizabeth stood with the ball in her hand, cheeks hot. Anjali was right about the remark. But now everyone was looking at her as the girl who needed rescuing, and she hadn't said a single word. After practice Anjali asked, "You okay? I was so angry for you." "I know. Thank you," Elizabeth said. "Next time, let me bowl at him first. Then back me up."

qa.a: Anjali may feel a little stung after being so angry on her behalf, but also understand what kind of help Elizabeth actually wants.

Thursday
Weekly review today. Suraj is on leave because his dad had surgery, and his idea, splitting the delivery routes by pin code, came up. Mehta presented it like it had dropped from the sky. "We've been thinking we could split routes..." Everyone nodded. I felt my pulse in my ears. Then I said, as normally as I could, "That's Suraj's proposal from the 3rd. He had the cost numbers too; I can forward them." Mehta paused, then said, "Yes, yes, Suraj's. Good." That was it. No drama.
At lunch, someone joked that Suraj "always has some family excuse". I said, "His dad's in hospital, yaar. Not an excuse." Silence, then someone changed the subject.
Not heroic. Just trying to make it normal.
Naveen

qa.a: Suraj would likely feel grateful and protected, knowing someone defended his work and his family situation while he was away.

Baljeet,
I owe you an honest letter, not another post.
In March, when you asked HR for a ramp at the side entrance, I wrote that long post about standing with my colleague and tagged the whole office. It got two hundred likes. I felt great. Then you asked me to come to the facilities meeting and speak, and I said I had a client call. I didn't. Then you asked me to sign the letter to the landlord, and I said I'd look at it. I never did.
When you told me last week, "You liked being seen helping more than helping," I was angry for a day. Then I reread my post, and it was mostly about me.
So: the meeting is Thursday. I'll be there, I'll sign, and if I get something wrong, tell me. I'll listen this time.
Lokesh

qa.a: It got two hundred likes.

qa.a: Lokesh commits to attending Thursday's meeting, signing the letter, and asking to be corrected, all of which cost more than a post.

qa.a: Baljeet would need Lokesh actually present and signing, since earlier promises faded as soon as effort was needed.

passage: You asked, Jasleen, so I'll be honest, even though it isn't flattering. Last year I got very loud about fair pay for the domestic workers in our housing society. Stories, a poster, a hashtag. I'm Alka, the girl with the "ally" sticker on her laptop. Then the residents' committee proposed an actual raise, and I realised it meant paying Sarojini-didi, who cooks for us, more every month. Suddenly I was busy on the meeting day. When Sarojini-didi asked if I'd speak for the workers, I said, "Let's see." She just looked at me. That look did something. I went to the next meeting, sat at the back, and mostly listened to the workers talk. One of them corrected me in front of everyone: I'd been calling it charity. It isn't. It's wages. I said, "You're right." That felt worse than the stickers, and much more real.

qa.q: What did Alka have on her laptop?
qa.a: An "ally" sticker.

qa.q: Why did Sarojini-didi's look affect Alka so much?
qa.a: It made Alka see that her loud support vanished once it cost her money, and she felt ashamed.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Alka's behaviour, and what did she change?
qa.a: After the look, she went to the next meeting, listened to the workers, and accepted a correction about charity versus wages.

qa.q: How might the workers see Alka at that second meeting?
qa.a: They might be cautious at first, remembering "Let's see", but someone who listens and says "You're right" is easier to trust than someone with stickers.

grounding: A young woman admits that her public support for workers' pay faded when it cost her, and describes learning to listen and accept correction.

passage: I'm Pooja, and I've watched Irfan since he joined our office's safety committee in January. At the town hall he took the mic and said, "As a man, I want to be an ally," and the room clapped. He posted a photo with the committee banner that same evening. Then came the actual work: checking late-night cab routes, three nights a month, till eleven. Irfan came once. When Shabnam from HR pointed out that his draft rule, "women should leave by eight", put the burden on women, he said, "I was only trying to help," and stopped replying in the group. I can't know what's going on inside him. Maybe he's busy. But the banner photo is still his profile picture, and the cab checks are down to three of us.

qa.a: "As a man, I want to be an ally."

qa.a: He may have felt embarrassed or criticised, which could be why he said "I was only trying to help" and went quiet.

qa.q: At the moment Shabnam corrected him, what choice could Irfan have made instead?
qa.a: He could have thanked Shabnam, asked how to rewrite the rule, and kept coming to the cab checks, staying through the discomfort.

qa.a: They're left doing the late-night checks with fewer hands, while his banner photo still earns him credit.
